title: Heh
hookLine: the breath sound, added to Abram and Sarai to make Abraham and Sarah

cards: "Neither shall thy name any more be called Abram, but thy name shall be Abraham." That's God speaking in Genesis, to a man already old who has been Abram all his life.
Later in the same chapter it happens again, to his wife: no more Sarai, from now on Sarah. Two new names, in a single conversation. In English it looks like a few letters shuffled.
In Hebrew the change is smaller, and stranger: each name gains the same letter, one that barely makes a sound. It's the letter you'd use to write a sigh.

teach.b: First, the sound. Say it with your hand in front of your mouth: heh. No tongue, no lips, no teeth, just warm air, about as close as speech comes to simply breathing out.

teach.h: AVRAHAM: A HEH IN THE MIDDLE.
teach.b: In Hebrew his name gains a heh in the middle and becomes Avraham, and the verse gives the reason in the same breath: "for the father of a multitude of nations have I made thee." A promise, sealed by adding a breath.
Third, Sarai. Her change works differently: the yud at the end comes off, and a heh takes its place.
"As for Sarai thy wife, thou shalt not call her name Sarai, but Sarah shall her name be." Husband and wife both carry the same new letter out of that conversation. Why heh?
Some answer that it's the letter of breath, and a new name is like a new breath of life. Some rabbis go further.
In the Talmud, in tractate Menachot, they take a word from Genesis about the heavens and the earth being created and split it in two: be-heh, with heh, and bera'am, he created them.
This world, they read, was made with the breath letter. Fourth, what it means for a person. Abraham and Sarah didn't get new faces or new families that day.

teach.h: THE SAME NAME, PLUS A BREATH.
teach.b: They got one breath added to who they already were. Not a new person. The same person, with a little more air in them.

how: Children learning the alef-bet may be taught heh by its soft h sound; the renaming of Abram and Sarai in Genesis 17 is read in synagogue as part of the cycle of Torah readings, and some teachers point out the added heh.

games.q: you're Sarai, and God is changing your husband's name with a new letter. what happens to yours?
o: it gains a second, different letter.
its last letter becomes the same breath letter, heh.
games.why: Sarai becomes Sarah: the yud comes off and a heh takes its place. husband and wife leave carrying the same new letter.

practice: Breathe in through your nose without forcing it, then let the air out through an open mouth, long and slow, so it makes the faintest sound: heh.

Do it again, letting the breath out be longer than the breath in, and if a name comes to mind, yours or someone you love, let it ride on the breath. If you pray, let the breath be a prayer without words.

wordCard.voice: Heh. The breath letter, the h sound, added to Abram and set in place of Sarai's last letter. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the letter heh, the h sound; also written הֵה.

carryVoice: Your line: heh is breath. A name can grow by one soft letter. I'll be here tomorrow.
